mean.when: the dimension is a general capability and several answers average out fairly

min.when: one bad answer in the dimension is disqualifying on its own

max.when: the dimension only needs one convincing demonstration

weighted_mean.when: the dimensions trade off, and a strong axis may fairly carry a weaker one

min_dimension.when: the company promises one thing, and a weak axis must not be carried by the others; weights are not read

cover_first.when: a dimension with no answer yet is worse than a shallow one, so a level pick goes to whatever is still owed

plan_order.when: the order the questions are written in is deliberate, so a level pick follows it and coverage is left to the reserve

reserve_debt.when: every dimension must be answered before any is answered twice, so turns are held back for what is still owed

free.when: the conversation leads and the budget ends it: a dimension may finish unanswered and be flagged uncovered, and because `done` only speaks once coverage is met, an interview that leaves one short runs to max_q

measured._note: Not written by the model, and not guessed: samples is a cost knob, and one call is the default; raise it only if your own records show Jev's spread moving a decision; noise_floor holds one measured spread per kind of question Jev is asked, because a Choice among questions and a Score against a rubric do not wobble by the same amount. Measure them against your own deployment with `python3 app.py --noise` — these were taken on jev-latest released 2026-09-10, 20 averaged groups per kind, on the record whose marks sat nearest the gate. A floor measured where Jev is already certain reads as roughly zero and trusts every close call, so --noise picks that record for you. All three are merged into a plan after generation. measurement_boundary is the score at which a Replay counts a change of side; it is for drift detection only and never decides anything about a person (ADR-0002).

intake._note: Jev screens the Brief before a model is paid to write a Plan from it (Q43).

work.true: the document says what the work actually is, concretely enough to ask about
work.false: the document only describes the company or the role in the abstract

values.true: the document says what it wants in a person, not only what it offers them
values.false: the document never says what would make someone right for this

gradable.true: there is enough here to tell a strong answer from a weak one
gradable.false: any answer would look equally good against this document

turn._note: The words Jev is asked with each turn. The two slots are the loop's structure and stay in app.py; `done`'s criteria are the Plan's, because what counts as enough is one Brief's question. `option` may use {dimension}, {text} and {context}, and nothing else.
turn.done: Judging by `job_context`, have we heard enough to assess this candidate?
turn.next: Given the answers so far, which question is now most worth asking?
turn.widget: Given `question_asked` and the answers so far, which input should this person be given to answer it with?

generation._note: The instruction given to the writing model. Kept here so the domain stays out of app.py.
generation.prompt:
You are writing the interview plan for one company, from the document below.

=== THE DOCUMENT ===
{brief}
=== END OF DOCUMENT ===

Write the plan in the same language the document is written in — including the
dimension names, which are shown to people and must read as the document's own
words, never as English identifiers.

Rules that matter more than they look:
- Dimensions come from what this document says it cares about. Do not import a generic
  competency list. Weights sum to 1.0 across the dimensions you choose.
- Every question belongs to exactly one dimension, and every dimension has at least two
  questions so a weak answer is not the whole of it.
- `context` says when this question is worth asking, given what has been heard so far.
  It is read by a small model choosing the next question, so describe the situation.
- Rubric levels describe concrete situations, worst first, not degrees of goodness.
  'Cannot give an example' beats 'poor'. Each level must stand on its own.
- Where a question asks what somebody has done, one level must be the answer that
  describes it well without having done it — fluent, correct, and not theirs. It is
  the commonest answer a strong talker gives, and a rubric with no level for it
  leaves the judge filing it at the top.
- `options` is null unless the question genuinely has a closed set of answers; then
  `ui` must be one that takes options.
- `fit.rubric` judges the whole person against this document, on the same shape of scale.
- Things the document says it does NOT care about must not become questions.
- min_q and max_q: enough turns to cover every dimension, with room to go deeper.
  max_q must exceed min_q or the interview can never end early.
- done.true and done.false: when has this interview heard enough to stop? Two situations
  in the document's own terms, not degrees. A small model reads them to decide whether
  to end the interview, so they must be checkable against the answers given.
- Write more questions than per_dimension x dimensions. With exactly that many, coverage
  is only satisfied by the very last answer and the interview can never end early.
- max_q must exceed per_dimension x dimensions PLUS reserve_early. At or below that,
  every turn is reserved for coverage from the first one, the judge never gets to
  choose what follows an answer, and the interview cannot adapt to anybody.
- reserve_early: how many turns early to start holding questions back for a dimension
  still owed an answer. 0 lets the judge pick freely until the budget only just covers
  what is owed; a number as large as max_q puts breadth before depth from the first turn.
  It changes the order questions are asked in, and which ones, if the interview ends
  before the budget runs out.
- per_dimension: how many answers every dimension must be scored on before the
  interview may end. 0 lets any question be asked at any time; 1 guarantees each
  dimension is touched; 2 keeps a dimension from resting on one answer, at the cost of
  a longer interview. It must fit the budget: per_dimension x dimensions <= max_q.
generation.supplement:
A company is hiring. Below is what it says it needs, then one applicant's own
account of their background. Write the questions worth asking THIS applicant that
the standard set does not already ask.

=== WHAT THE COMPANY NEEDS ===
{brief}
=== END ===

=== THE APPLICANT'S OWN ACCOUNT ===
{resume}
=== END ===

=== THE STANDARD SET ALREADY ASKS THESE ===
{asked}
=== END ===

Write in the same language the company's document is written in.

- 2 to {most} questions. Fewer is better than padded.
- Each one must come from something specific in this applicant's account — a claim
  to test, a gap to ask about, a strength worth going deeper on. A question that
  would fit any applicant is not worth asking here.
- The standard set above has its subjects covered. A question landing on a subject
  already listed there is wasted however differently it is worded — that subject gets
  answered anyway. Spend these few on what only this account raises, and on nothing
  the standard set would have reached without it.
- `dimension` must be exactly one of: {dimensions}
- `id` must start with `x_`.
- `context` says when this is worth asking given what has been heard so far.
- `options` is null. Set it only if the question genuinely has a closed set of
  answers to pick from, and then `ui` must be one that takes options. It is not
  a place for the rubric — the rubric goes in `rubric`.
- Rubric levels describe concrete situations, worst first, and there must be
  exactly {levels} of them so they read on the same scale as the rest.
- Where the question asks what they did, one level must be the answer that describes
  it well without having done it. A question built on something in their own account
  is exactly where that turns up — including the answer that withdraws the claim the
  question was built on.
- Re-read the part of the document saying what it does not look at, and check each
  question against it before writing it down.
- A gap the applicant states is a reason to ask what they did about it — what they
  reached for, who they asked, what it cost them. It is not a reason to ask them to
  speculate about the thing they have not done: that answer only tests who talks well.
